article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, better known as the Rebbe , is having his story told in a documentary feature from the team behind The Journey of Menachem Begin and Centered: Joe Lieberman .

The doc, The Emissary of Light , has rolled cameras and will document the transformative leader of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement. The Rebbe’s teachings influenced millions and he was recognized with awards by both Bill Clinton and George W. Bush.

The documentary film will tell the Rebbe’s story through one of his most visible, and most contested, ideas: the public menorah. To the Rebbe, Hanukkah’s light was meant to be seen, not kept behind closed doors. When giant menorahs began rising in public squares across America, they ignited a national fight over how visible Jewish life should be, placing both the question and the man behind it at the center of American public life.

Related Stories

James Gunn Claps Back At Critics Of Continuity In His DCU

Donald Trump Posts 1,300+ Word Sunday Night Diatribe About "Complete And Total Loser" Bill Maher, Nine Days After Praising Their "Great Dinner"

The Rebbe corresponded with Bush, Ronald Reagan, Jimmy Carter and Gerald Ford. Clinton posthumously awarded him the Congressional Gold Medal for his moral leadership and Bush invited a group of Rabbis to the Oval Office to recognize him for his commitment to education, also posthumously.

Watch on Deadline

“What drew me to the Rebbe was the extraordinary influence one man could have on the world,” said director Rachel Greenberg . “The public menorah offers a window into his larger vision: a belief that Jewish identity should be embraced openly and that every person, regardless of faith or background, has a responsibility to make a difference. Through this film, we will explore the man behind that vision, how he inspired others to bring it to life, and what his example can teach us about our own capacity to make a difference.”

The Rebbe: Emissary of Light is directed and produced by Greenberg, the producer behind Upheaval: The Journey of Menachem Begin and Centered: Joe Lieberman . Rob Schwartz, who also produced Upheaval and Centered and founded non-profit film production studio Hidden Light Institute, serves as an executive producer on The Rebbe , as well. Additional executive producers include George Rohr, Jonathan Tratt, and Igor Tulchinsky, with The Marcia and Stanley Reiter Family Foundation serving as a producer.

article_text:
News

Tammy Nguyen's New Opera Will Be the Coda to the Venice Biennale

The artist will present an aria from the still-unfinished opera, “Timaeus and The Teacher,” during the festival's closing program.

Timaeus and the Teacher at Wesleyan University (photo Elisabeth Bernstein, courtesy the artist and Lehmann Maupin)

Artist Tammy Nguyen will present the foreword to her debut opera Timaeus and The Teacher at the 61st Venice Biennale's closing program on November 13 and 14, capping off an eventful edition of the international contemporary art festival.

The aria is the entry point to Nguyen's still-unfinished opera, which traces the national and ideological impacts of the Vietnam War and fuses Plato’s theories of the cosmos with enduring questions of identity. Inspired by her father's experiences as a refugee aboard a vessel in the South China Sea, Nguyen centers the performance around a Vietnamese English teacher who attempts to flee Saigon (since renamed to Ho Chi Minh City) by boat, two years after North Vietnamese forces captured the capital in 1975. Grammy-nominated tenor Brian Vu will sing the libretto as the titular teacher, while a group of dancers will maneuver around him with a tapestry composed of flags.

“I was really fascinated by what happened at sea, as are many children of refugees from war-torn countries,” Nguyen told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. “The South China Sea is such a heavily trafficked area, and it created little stories where humans and the global economy collided.”

Commissioned and produced by Wesleyan University, where Nguyen teaches as an associate professor, the opera echoes themes prevalent in the artist’s other works , including a series of paintings on view at the biennale's Central Pavilion through November 22.

The tapestry of flags at the heart of the performance extends upon Nguyen's 2024 exhibition Timaeus and the Nations at the Sarasota Art Museum, where the artist rearranged 46 "flags of convenience," alluding to the practice in which ship operators change their flags for tax and regulation benefits.

Choreographed by Jamal Jackson, the opera's dancers will configure the tapestry into mountain ranges, a ship, the sea, and the cosmological diagram championed by the Pythagorean philosopher of Plato’s dialogue, Timaeus.

“Opera has a gestalt of sorts, just this massive tapestry of coming together and telling a story,” said Nguyen, adding that she's had the goal of directing an opera since learning to play and write music in San Francisco. “I took the anthems of all the countries in the flags of convenience, extracted various lyrics, and hybridized them arbitrarily for the libretto.”

As Vu’s character journeys across the sea, musical accompaniments mirror his literal and ideological movements. Nguyen assembled the libretto by breaking down traditional English language structures through a fractal sequence, while composer Neely Bruce remixed national anthems into the musical score.

Other performances slated for the final days of the biennale include a gathering around a Ouija board led by Hagar Ophir, stories of cultivation and global exchange with Lebanese artists Ziad Antar, Hatem Imam and Nayla Mabsout, and a meditation on salt as an essential mineral from Nathalie Vairac. While it’s unclear when the full production of the opera will be presented to audiences, Nguyen aims to have it completed by Bruce’s 85th birthday, in fall of 2029.

“The idea of nationhood is so flexible,” Nguyen stated. “But people die over it and fight over it, questioning whether they belong. We grapple with these questions all the time, as people who are looking to feel at home or develop a sense of agency for ourselves.”

title_original: Attend, the First Marketplace Connecting Filmmakers Directly to Theater Owners, Finally Launches Today
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Way back in October 2024, The Fithian Group, led by former NATO chief John Fithian and founding partner Patrick Corcoran, announced plans for an ambitious new marketplace , one that would help connect filmmakers and their projects directly to theater owners looking to book their movies and effectively cut out the distribution middleman. Today, that vision is now a reality.", "links": [{"text": "John Fithian", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/john-fithian/"}, {"text": "announced plans for an ambitious new marketplace", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/business/former-nato-chief-launches-platform-get-indie-films-into-theaters-attend-john-fithian-1235061412/"}, {"text": "connect filmmakers and their projects directly to theater owners", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/business/john-fithian-attend-indie-distribution-interview-1235093741/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Fithian Group on Wednesday at the American Film Market announced the formal launch of Attend Theatrical Marketplace, the group’s online platform and marketplace for filmmakers and exhibitors that is now live and ready for business.", "links": [{"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}, {"text": "Attend", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/attend/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Attend launches with today just a curated selection of four films, all of whose filmmakers will now be doing the legwork to connect with theaters and find venues at which to exhibit their work. But the platform is already loaded with exhibition partners who will be able to browse available films, with more to be added soon, and Attend will eventually be a fully open platform to any filmmaker who wishes to do outreach directly to theater owners."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/James-Gunn.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "SAN DIEGO, CALIFORNIA - JULY 23: James Gunn speaks onstage at the Marvel Cinematic Universe Mega-Panel during 2022 Comic-Con International Day 3 at San Diego Convention Center on July 23, 2022 in San Diego, California. (Photo by Daniel Knighton/Getty Images)", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Screenshot-2026-05-11-at-1.56.37 PM.png?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Paper Tiger", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "IndieWire got an early demo of Attend and how it aims to simplify the work that distributors do every day in putting movies into theaters, as well as the work exhibitors have to do in booking movies, paying invoices, and more. And IndieWire will on Wednesday lead a panel discussion at AFM with Corcoran, Charles Beale of the site’s designer Titlepool, and filmmaker Lilian T. Mehrel, whose Tribeca award-winning film “Honeyjoon” will be one of the four inaugural films shopping for theaters.", "links": [{"text": "panel discussion at AFM", "url": "https://americanfilmmarket.com/sessions/the-attend-theatrical-marketplace-and-how-technology-will-transform-independent-film-distribution/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Beyond “Honeyjoon,” the other three films available on Attend at launch are Kenny Riches’ crime drama “Mouse”; “Spoke,” which is a documentary about firefighters and the trauma they deal with after the fires; and “Censurada,” an LGBTQ+ drama from Marco Garza about forbidden love in 1969 Spain."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The vision of Attend was outlined to IndieWire over a year ago with an indie rom-com called “You, Me, and Her” serving as an early guinea pig for the idea . The thinking was, if you had a film that could demonstrate it already had an audience and you had a clear sense of where your audience was and how to target them, all you needed were the screens to showcase your movie and the means to get your movie into the hands of those theaters.", "links": [{"text": "“You, Me, and Her” serving as an early guinea pig for the idea", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/business/you-me-her-20-brand-partners-selina-ringel-interview-1235092328/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That was and remains the tricky part. Few people have the connections with theater owners to be able to reach them and get a film out in any meaningful capacity. This year has produced a number of examples in which enterprising filmmakers have done without distributors and found the audience they already knew was there to release their movies. YouTuber Markiplier went directly to theaters and made $50 million with his horror movie “Iron Lung.” The documentary “NAZA” skipped a distributor in order to get its story about the IDF out with urgency. Even an AI movie called “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is next month releasing without the aid of a distributor.", "links": [{"text": "found the audience they already knew was there", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/analysis/how-much-is-your-audience-worth-in-development-1235204461/"}, {"text": "YouTuber Markiplier went directly to theaters", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/analysis/markiplier-iron-lung-self-distribution-box-office-interview-1235177520/"}, {"text": "“NAZA” skipped a distributor", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/box-office/naza-documentary-israel-gaza-crosses-500k-self-distributed-1235221331/"}, {"text": "AI movie called “Gods Don’t Give Gifts”", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/news/breaking-news/ai-movie-gods-dont-give-gifts-grimes-cameo-times-square-1235225119/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Attend seeks to use technology to simplify that process, to get your film out to an even wider audience and a more targeted one. article_text:
Way back in October 2024, The Fithian Group, led by former NATO chief John Fithian and founding partner Patrick Corcoran, announced plans for an ambitious new marketplace , one that would help connect filmmakers and their projects directly to theater owners looking to book their movies and effectively cut out the distribution middleman. Today, that vision is now a reality.

The Fithian Group on Wednesday at the American Film Market announced the formal launch of Attend Theatrical Marketplace, the group’s online platform and marketplace for filmmakers and exhibitors that is now live and ready for business.

Attend launches with today just a curated selection of four films, all of whose filmmakers will now be doing the legwork to connect with theaters and find venues at which to exhibit their work. But the platform is already loaded with exhibition partners who will be able to browse available films, with more to be added soon, and Attend will eventually be a fully open platform to any filmmaker who wishes to do outreach directly to theater owners.

IndieWire got an early demo of Attend and how it aims to simplify the work that distributors do every day in putting movies into theaters, as well as the work exhibitors have to do in booking movies, paying invoices, and more. And IndieWire will on Wednesday lead a panel discussion at AFM with Corcoran, Charles Beale of the site’s designer Titlepool, and filmmaker Lilian T. Mehrel, whose Tribeca award-winning film “Honeyjoon” will be one of the four inaugural films shopping for theaters.

Beyond “Honeyjoon,” the other three films available on Attend at launch are Kenny Riches’ crime drama “Mouse”; “Spoke,” which is a documentary about firefighters and the trauma they deal with after the fires; and “Censurada,” an LGBTQ+ drama from Marco Garza about forbidden love in 1969 Spain.

The vision of Attend was outlined to IndieWire over a year ago with an indie rom-com called “You, Me, and Her” serving as an early guinea pig for the idea . The thinking was, if you had a film that could demonstrate it already had an audience and you had a clear sense of where your audience was and how to target them, all you needed were the screens to showcase your movie and the means to get your movie into the hands of those theaters.

That was and remains the tricky part. Few people have the connections with theater owners to be able to reach them and get a film out in any meaningful capacity. This year has produced a number of examples in which enterprising filmmakers have done without distributors and found the audience they already knew was there to release their movies. YouTuber Markiplier went directly to theaters and made $50 million with his horror movie “Iron Lung.” The documentary “NAZA” skipped a distributor in order to get its story about the IDF out with urgency. Even an AI movie called “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is next month releasing without the aid of a distributor.

Attend seeks to use technology to simplify that process, to get your film out to an even wider audience and a more targeted one. For filmmakers, the platform is designed to eliminate the guesswork of who you need to talk to, how you reach them, and what attributes a given exhibitor is looking for in a film. For exhibitors, it filters all your titles and screens into one place, and it makes the receiving of deliverables or the payment of invoices more automated than the often tedious work it is for most exhibitors today. It’s exciting to see the whole vision come into fruition.

On the filmmaker end, the way Attend works is you as an individual can upload details and assets about your film, from simple details like its runtime, logline, and genre, to much more granular details about the aspect ratio, the available formats, the awards it has won and festivals it has played, the social networking reach of talent, and many more data points. There may be assets you don’t realize will be significant to a given exhibitor but will jump out as they browse your profile. You can then identify themes that speak to the film’s target audience and narrow the demographics for which your film is intended.

From there, you can filter and browse theaters to identify which theaters would be the best fit for your movie. For instance, Attend has data that can show a theater is within walking distance of a firehouse or that the theater has ties to a local advocacy group that aligns with the themes of the film’s story, and Attend’s predictive AI engine can recommend those theaters that would be available and the best fit for your film. Then, instead of reaching out to each of those theaters individually, filmmakers can easily select all the relevant theaters they want to message and have the option to manually add or subtract more beyond the recommended targets. You can even modify proposed theatrical terms for individual theaters or personalize messages, and as theaters come in, Attend can dynamically estimate P&A spend for those locations.

When theater owners are contacted, they’ll receive push notifications about films that are available for them to review, and they can further browse any available films in the marketplace and do their own outreach. Exhibitors can create tabs and info on any number of their circuit’s screens or locations and can upload in spreadsheets specs like screen size, audio, and seat count that filmmakers can view themselves to better get a sense of which theaters are the best fit. Exhibitors can specify rental prices for individual screens, you can mark your theater as being willing to offer simple four-walling options or that it’s capable of hosting big premieres, whether you want to offer “split screens” or “clean screens,” or you can set terms for how long you’re able to hold a movie. And not only does it also itemize marketing costs, Attend clearly indicates what the share of a film’s box office would be if they were to accept it and program it.

This helps theater owners in a number of ways. It takes the busy work out of things like paying numerous individual vendors or distribution partners, and it lets you download and easily generate a W9 form based on that film’s booking, being able to do so across multiple locations. But for theater owners that generally don’t know what they’re playing until the Monday before, this gives theaters far more advanced leeway and awareness to then be able to do the necessary marketing, put tickets on sale, and actually get butts in seats. All that is especially important for the smaller indies that need that word of mouth.

For now, theaters haven’t linked their loyalty data or other point of sales or scheduling tools to Attend, but that could come with time, and as people actually begin to use the platform, the predictive functionality will improve in the long run.

Corcoran and Fithian see Attend being useful for smaller distributors themselves in the long run, not just individual filmmakers who want to cut out the middleman. Distributors can use it to plan the campaigns of multiple titles and use its automation features to save time and costs. And while today Attend just supports new releases, there’s no reason why older library titles couldn’t be marketed here to exhibitors as well.

Time will tell if filmmakers find Attend an effective form of reaching theaters or if exhibitors adopt the platform widely to make it a useful tool for all parties. But it’s an ambitious vision that if implemented properly could have enormous impacts for the independent film world. And after two years of effort and hype, that day could finally be here.

article_text:
Dal 29 ottobre al 1° novembre 2026 torna a Torino The Others Art Fair , la fiera dedicata alle pratiche artistiche emergenti e indipendenti. La 15ma edizione riunirà 53 espositori italiani e internazionali, tra gallerie, editori e progetti speciali, in una nuova sede: il piano terra del Parcheggio Lancia, in piazzale Chiribiri, nel quartiere Borgo San Paolo.

La scelta dello spazio è strettamente legata al tema dell’edizione, Sosta Temporanea. Forme di permanenza in uno spazio di passaggio . Un luogo progettato per l’attesa, la custodia e il transito delle automobili viene trasformato in uno spazio per l’arte contemporanea, proseguendo una linea che ha caratterizzato The Others fin dalla nascita: utilizzare edifici e infrastrutture non convenzionali come dispositivi espositivi. L’utilizzo del Parcheggio Lancia è reso possibile dalla collaborazione con GTT – Gruppo Torinese Trasporti, che ha concesso la struttura su indicazione dell’amministrazione comunale.

Un parcheggio diventa spazio espositivo

La scelta del Parcheggio Lancia assume un significato particolare anche perché coincide con i 15 anni di The Others. Nel corso della propria storia, la fiera ha costruito parte della sua identità proprio attraverso l’occupazione temporanea di luoghi in disuso e spazi inattesi, spesso preferendo contesti estranei alla tradizionale architettura fieristica, come nel caso, tra gli altri, degli ex Ospedali Regina Maria Adelaide e Alessandro Riberie.

Il rapporto con la trasformazione urbana sarà quindi uno dei fili conduttori anche dell’edizione 2026. L’architettura del Parcheggio Lancia non fungerà soltanto da contenitore. Le caratteristiche industriali della struttura e, in particolare, la grande rampa elicoidale che richiama in scala ridotta quella del Lingotto, entreranno direttamente nella costruzione del percorso fieristico.

La sede ha già ospitato iniziative culturali come TUTTOLIBERO , progetto promosso dalla Fondazione Merz e condiviso con MAUTO – Museo Nazionale dell’Automobile, Città di Torino, GTT e IREN. Con The Others, l’infrastruttura viene nuovamente sollevata, in via temporanea, dalla sua funzione ordinaria per diventare luogo di incontro tra gallerie, artist run spaces, spazi indipendenti, curatori, progetti interdisciplinari e pubblico.

«L’obiettivo di The Others è sempre stato portare l’arte contemporanea al di fuori dei classici centri culturali cittadini», spiegano i fondatori Roberto Casiraghi e Paola Rampini , sottolineando come questi luoghi possano instaurare un rapporto diretto tra architettura e contenuto. Nel caso del Parcheggio Lancia, aggiungono, «Il parcheggio cessa di essere una mera area di transito automobilistico. Si ferma, per diventare un nucleo accessibile di sperimentazione e cultura».

53 espositori tra ricerca emergente e spazi indipendenti

Saranno 53 gli espositori annunciati per l’edizione 2026, provenienti dall’Italia e dall’estero e distribuiti tra gallerie, realtà indipendenti, editoria e progetti speciali. Le proposte attraversano pittura, fotografia, scultura e collage, con ricerche dedicate, tra gli altri temi, alla trasformazione della materia e del paesaggio, alla memoria e alle relazioni tra individuo, ambiente e tempo. La pluralità dei linguaggi mantiene così la vocazione originaria della fiera, nata per offrire visibilità a realtà più giovani, sperimentali o laterali rispetto ai circuiti maggiormente consolidati del mercato.

Il tema della «sosta» viene interpretato anche in questa direzione: non soltanto come caratteristica funzionale del luogo ma come invito a rallentare lo sguardo, interrompendo temporaneamente la velocità con cui immagini e oggetti vengono normalmente consumati.

Una nuova sezione dedicata all’editoria

Tra le novità della 15ma edizione figura uno spazio specificamente dedicato all’editoria. Libri d’artista, pubblicazioni indipendenti e progetti editoriali affiancheranno le proposte delle gallerie, ampliando il confronto tra arti visive e altri linguaggi della produzione contemporanea. Una parte della sezione sarà inoltre riservata all’editoria per l’infanzia, con l’obiettivo di coinvolgere pubblici differenti e utilizzare il libro come strumento di avvicinamento alle pratiche artistiche contemporanee.

"https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/dick-clark-new-years-rockin-eve-simulcast-disney-plus-abc-1236904595/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他告诉《综艺》：“我是个女权主义者。我是个知识分子。我发现自己非常被这种超级阳刚的表演所吸引。”“我本该更懂事的，对吧？所以问题就在于：为什么我会这么着迷？”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "穆斯塔法将这种好奇心与一种想要调查他所认为的本质错误事物的愿望区分开来。当他在2016年着手这个项目时，他是将其作为对男子气概及其在不同语境下如何表达的人类学和社会学研究来进行的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他自己的成长经历为他提供了一个参考点。穆斯塔法在一个他所描述的开罗“本地”社区长大，周围充满了这种阳刚的准则。作为一个爱学习的“书呆子”，在那里他可能会被认为不够有男子气概。但当他进入牙医学校时，同样的表现反而会让他显得浮夸或粗俗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种反差帮助他认识到男子气概如何随语境而变化，这一事实他在他所观察的男性身上也看到了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他说：“他们在舞台上表现出的男子气概，与在酒吧门前不同，与他们在处理问题时不同，与他和家人在一起时也不同。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最初的探索花了大约3年时间才演变成一部电影，随着穆斯塔法与这些男性的关系加深，他被迫审视自己对男子气概的看法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种关系也影响了《大男孩不哭》的制作方式。穆斯塔法拒绝认为纪录片制作可以完全是纯粹旁观的，他认为镜头不可避免地会改变它前面发生的事情。这些男性成为了合作者，有时他们自己也会提议一些情境。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我不会说这部电影是我一个人拍的。我会说我是和片中的人物一起拍的。我们是一起完成的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "影片的核心人物之一是阿卜杜拉（Abdallah），拍摄开始前，穆斯塔法与他相处了一年。穆斯塔法最初以为这部电影将由关于男子气概的理念驱动，结果却在剪辑中发现，他们之间的友谊已成为影片的情感纽带。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Muhammad-Mustapha.jpg?w=1000", "alt": "", "caption": "穆罕默德·穆斯塔法，图源：Hassala Films", "credit": "Variety · Film", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他回忆道：“我曾以为电影里没有情感弧光。它是高度主题驱动的，而且非常形而上。”“最后，在剪辑时，我发现这部电影的情感核心其实是我们之间的友谊。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "建立这种关系也意味着赋予这些男性对他们所分享内容的控制权。参与者可以在整个制作过程中（包括最终剪辑阶段）要求删除某些素材。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他坚定地表示：“我赢得了他们的信任。这不是白白给我的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "女性的缺席同样是刻意安排的。穆斯塔法希望在一个全男性的环境中观察这些男性，他将其比作偷窥健身房的更衣室。他认为，引入女性会“改变这个等式”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对穆斯塔法而言，《大男孩不哭》核心探讨的问题远远超出了埃及的范畴。虽然男子气概在不同文化中呈现出不同的形式，但他认为对男性情感表达的限制具有痛苦的普遍性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他辩称：“男人被允许表达的唯一情绪就是愤怒。”“想象一下，由于所有这些情绪的压抑，男性的心理变得多么扭曲。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "埃尔古纳的首映使《大男孩不哭》回到了其发展过程中的一个重要节点。早在2020年，穆斯塔法就带着这个项目参加了该电影节的产业分支——CineGouna，此后该项目获得了多哈电影学院、红海电影基金以及德国罗伯特·博世基金会（Robert Bosch Foundation）的支持。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他反思道：“这是一个完美的圆满时刻。我很兴奋能把它展示给埃及的观众，尽管我稍稍有点紧张。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "长达10年的电影开发历程也促使穆斯塔法反思埃及及该地区的独立电影是如何制作的。他希望电影人能承担更多艺术风险，并将目光聚焦于本土观众，而不是国际电影节和节目策划人的奇思妙想。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们需要用更少的预算、承担更少的财务风险，但去冒更多的艺术风险。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最重要的是：“把我们的故事讲给我们的观众听。”", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Egyptian filmmaker Muhammad Mustapha ’s “Big Boys Don’t Cry” follows a group of Cairo bodybuilders and nightclub bouncers, offering a view into how men understand and perform masculinity.", "links": [{"text": "Muhammad Mustapha", "url": "https://variety.com/t/muhammad-mustapha/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The documentary, which had its world premiere in the Feature Documentary Competition at Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival , grew out of Mustapha’s curiosity about this particular group of men and questions about his own understanding of masculinity.", "links": [{"text": "El Gouna Film Festival", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/film/global/el-gouna-andrew-mohsen-discovery-arab-cinema-cinegouna-1236913914/"}]}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Related Stories"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/051325CT2MB-09036.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "Throughout Disneyland Resort in Anaheim, Calif., vibrant colors and bold banners take over Disneyland Park, Disney California Adventure Park, Downtown Disney District and the Hotels of Disneyland Resort. Themed décor such as a 50-foot sculpture inspired by the Sleeping Beauty Castle will be in the Esplanade, while the floral Mickey is adorned with vibrant flowers. Guests can \"celebrate happy” during the limited-time Disneyland Resort 70th Celebration beginning May 16, 2025. (Christian Thompson/Disneyland Resort)", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Disney Bids on Character.AI Assets as Chatbot Provider Files for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy", "links": [{"text": "Disney Bids on Character.AI Assets as Chatbot Provider Files for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/biz/news/disney-bids-on-character-ai-assets-chapter-11-bankruptcy-1236909984/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Ryan-Seacrest-Rita-Ora-PKB-KBU_7977.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "Rita Ora and Ryan Seacrest during \"Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve With Ryan Seacrest 2026\" held in Times Square Ball on December 31, 2025 in New York City, New York.", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "'Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve With Ryan Seacrest' to Simulcast on Both ABC and Disney+ for the First Time", "links": [{"text": "'Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve With Ryan Seacrest' to Simulcast on Both ABC and Disney+ for the First Time", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/tv/news/dick-clark-new-years-rockin-eve-simulcast-disney-plus-abc-1236904595/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I’m a feminist. I’m intellectual. I find myself very drawn to this hyper-masculine performance,” he tells Variety . “I should know better, right? And so this was the question: Why am I so intrigued?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mustapha distinguishes that curiosity from a desire to investigate something he saw as inherently wrong. When he began the project in 2016, he approached it as an anthropological and sociological study of masculinity and how it is expressed in different contexts."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "His own upbringing gave him a point of reference. Mustapha grew up in what he describes as a “local” Cairo neighborhood, where he was surrounded by its masculine codes. As a studious “nerd,” he could be seen as less masculine there. But when he entered dental school, the same behavior could instead make him appear loud or vulgar."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That contrast helped him recognize how masculinity could shift according to context, a fact he also saw among the men he was observing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“How they perform their masculinity on stage is different than in front of the pub, is different than when he is addressing a problem, different than when he is with his family,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It took roughly three years for that initial exploration to develop into a film, as Mustapha’s relationship with the men deepened and he was forced to examine his own views of masculinity."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That relationship also informed how “Big Boys Don’t Cry” was made. Mustapha rejects the idea that documentary filmmaking can ever be entirely observational, arguing that a camera inevitably changes what happens in front of it. The men became collaborators, at times proposing situations themselves."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I wouldn’t say I made this film alone. I would say I made it with the characters. We made it together.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One of the film’s central figures is Abdallah, with whom Mustapha spent a year before filming began. Mustapha initially believed the film would be driven by its ideas about masculinity, only to discover in the edit that their friendship had become its emotional throughline."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Muhammad-Mustapha.jpg?w=1000", "alt": "", "caption": "Muhammad Mustapha Courtesy of Hassala Films", "credit": "Variety · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I thought there was no emotional arc in the film. It was very theme-driven, and it was very intellectual,” he recalls. “At the end, while we were editing, I discovered that the emotional core of the film is actually our friendship.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Building that relationship also meant giving the men control over what they shared. Participants could ask for material to be removed throughout the process, including during the final edit."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I earned their trust. It was not given to me,” he affirms."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The absence of women is equally intentional. Mustapha wanted to observe the men in an exclusively male environment, which he compares to peeking into a gym locker room. Introducing women, he believed, would “change the equation.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For Mustapha, the questions at the heart of “Big Boys Don’t Cry” extend far beyond Egypt. While masculinity takes different forms across cultures, he sees restrictions on men’s emotional expression as painfully universal."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“The only emotion men are allowed to express is anger,” he argues. “Imagine how distorted the male psyche is because of all this suppression of emotions.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The El Gouna premiere brings “Big Boys Don’t Cry” back to a major stop in its development. Mustapha brought the project to CineGouna, the festival’s industry arm, in 2020 before it went on to receive support from the Doha Film Institute, Red Sea Film Fund and Germany’s Robert Bosch Foundation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“It’s a full circle moment,” he reflects. “I’m very excited to show it to people in Egypt, though I’m slightly nervous.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The film’s decade-long development has also led Mustapha to reflect on how independent films are made in Egypt and the region. article_text:
Egyptian filmmaker Muhammad Mustapha ’s “Big Boys Don’t Cry” follows a group of Cairo bodybuilders and nightclub bouncers, offering a view into how men understand and perform masculinity.

The documentary, which had its world premiere in the Feature Documentary Competition at Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival , grew out of Mustapha’s curiosity about this particular group of men and questions about his own understanding of masculinity.

“I’m a feminist. I’m intellectual. I find myself very drawn to this hyper-masculine performance,” he tells Variety . “I should know better, right? And so this was the question: Why am I so intrigued?”

Mustapha distinguishes that curiosity from a desire to investigate something he saw as inherently wrong. When he began the project in 2016, he approached it as an anthropological and sociological study of masculinity and how it is expressed in different contexts.

His own upbringing gave him a point of reference. Mustapha grew up in what he describes as a “local” Cairo neighborhood, where he was surrounded by its masculine codes. As a studious “nerd,” he could be seen as less masculine there. But when he entered dental school, the same behavior could instead make him appear loud or vulgar.

That contrast helped him recognize how masculinity could shift according to context, a fact he also saw among the men he was observing.

“How they perform their masculinity on stage is different than in front of the pub, is different than when he is addressing a problem, different than when he is with his family,” he says.

It took roughly three years for that initial exploration to develop into a film, as Mustapha’s relationship with the men deepened and he was forced to examine his own views of masculinity.

That relationship also informed how “Big Boys Don’t Cry” was made. Mustapha rejects the idea that documentary filmmaking can ever be entirely observational, arguing that a camera inevitably changes what happens in front of it. The men became collaborators, at times proposing situations themselves.

“I wouldn’t say I made this film alone. I would say I made it with the characters. We made it together.”

One of the film’s central figures is Abdallah, with whom Mustapha spent a year before filming began. Mustapha initially believed the film would be driven by its ideas about masculinity, only to discover in the edit that their friendship had become its emotional throughline.

“I thought there was no emotional arc in the film. It was very theme-driven, and it was very intellectual,” he recalls. “At the end, while we were editing, I discovered that the emotional core of the film is actually our friendship.”

Building that relationship also meant giving the men control over what they shared. Participants could ask for material to be removed throughout the process, including during the final edit.

“I earned their trust. It was not given to me,” he affirms.

The absence of women is equally intentional. Mustapha wanted to observe the men in an exclusively male environment, which he compares to peeking into a gym locker room. Introducing women, he believed, would “change the equation.”

For Mustapha, the questions at the heart of “Big Boys Don’t Cry” extend far beyond Egypt. While masculinity takes different forms across cultures, he sees restrictions on men’s emotional expression as painfully universal.

“The only emotion men are allowed to express is anger,” he argues. “Imagine how distorted the male psyche is because of all this suppression of emotions.”

The El Gouna premiere brings “Big Boys Don’t Cry” back to a major stop in its development. Mustapha brought the project to CineGouna, the festival’s industry arm, in 2020 before it went on to receive support from the Doha Film Institute, Red Sea Film Fund and Germany’s Robert Bosch Foundation.

“It’s a full circle moment,” he reflects. “I’m very excited to show it to people in Egypt, though I’m slightly nervous.”

The film’s decade-long development has also led Mustapha to reflect on how independent films are made in Egypt and the region. He wants filmmakers to take more artistic risks and focus on local audiences rather than on the whims of international festivals and programmers.

“We need to work with less budget, with less financial risk, and more artistic risks.”

And above all: “Tell our stories to our audience.”
